note: Original IELTS Passage-3-style excerpts written for LinguaFlow. Markup: {id:text} = obvious pair (pre-highlighted), [id:text] = keyword the learner pairs, [g:____] = gap. pairs[id].p = phrase in the passage (null = not in the passage), n = which occurrence.

sets.title: The fixation on metrics
sets.topic: Quản lý công · đo lường hiệu suất
sets.passage: Few administrative habits have spread as relentlessly as the urge to quantify. Hospitals, universities and police forces are now routinely assessed through performance indicators, on the assumption that what can be counted can also be improved. The economist Charles Goodhart observed as early as 1975 that once a measure is turned into a target, it ceases to be a reliable measure, because those being assessed learn to manipulate the figures rather than the reality behind them. His warning has been largely ignored. Critics such as Jerry Muller argue that the problem is not measurement itself but the fixation on it: numerical data, they contend, are indispensable when they inform the judgement of experienced practitioners, yet corrosive when they are used to replace it. Muller concedes that metrics have occasionally exposed genuine failings, notably in surgical outcomes, where publishing mortality rates prompted some underperforming units to reform. Nevertheless, he notes that the same publication led a number of surgeons to decline high-risk patients altogether, so as to protect their statistics.

items.stmt: {gd:Goodhart} was the [fi:first person] to [no:notice] that [tg:targets] can [ds:distort] measurement.

fi.vi: bài chỉ nói 'as early as 1975', không nói 'đầu tiên'

ds.p: ceases to be a reliable measure
ds.vi: không còn đáng tin = bị bóp méo

items.explain: Mọi ý đều khớp TRỪ 'first person'. 'As early as 1975' chỉ nói là sớm, không nói ông là người đầu tiên. Pill không có cặp → NOT GIVEN.

items.stmt: {gw:Goodhart's warning} has had [li:little influence].
items.explain: 'Largely ignored' (phần lớn bị phớt lờ) = 'little influence' (ít ảnh hưởng). Đồng nghĩa → TRUE.

items.stmt: {mu:Muller} believes that {nd:numerical data} should [np:play no part] in [pj:professional decision-making].

pj.vi: phán đoán của người hành nghề có kinh nghiệm

items.explain: Muller nói dữ liệu là 'indispensable' (không thể thiếu) khi hỗ trợ phán đoán của chuyên gia. 'Play no part' (không có vai trò gì) trái nghĩa → FALSE.

items.stmt: According to Muller, {mt:metrics} have [nv:never revealed] [rp:real problems].
items.explain: 'Occasionally exposed' (đôi khi đã phơi bày) mâu thuẫn với 'never revealed' (chưa bao giờ). Bẫy: từ 'concedes' (thừa nhận) – Muller chấp nhận một phần điểm tốt của metrics.

items.stmt: {pm:Publishing mortality rates} caused some surgeons to [av:avoid treating] [dc:dangerous cases].
items.explain: 'The same publication' = việc công bố tỉ lệ tử vong. 'Decline high-risk patients' = 'avoid treating dangerous cases' → TRUE.

sets.title: Rewriting the past: memory reconsolidation
sets.topic: Khoa học thần kinh · trí nhớ
sets.passage: For most of the twentieth century, neuroscientists believed that a memory, once consolidated, was stored in a more or less permanent form, much as a document is filed in an archive. Experiments conducted around the turn of the millennium challenged this view. Researchers found that when rats were prompted to recall a fearful association, the memory temporarily became unstable, and administering a drug that blocked protein synthesis at that moment could weaken it substantially. Recollection, in other words, appeared to reopen a memory for revision before it was stored again – a process now termed reconsolidation. The implications are considerable. On the one hand, the finding offers a plausible mechanism for the well-documented unreliability of eyewitness testimony, since each act of remembering creates an opportunity for distortion. On the other, it has raised hopes that traumatic memories might be deliberately modified, although clinical trials have so far produced inconsistent results, and some ethicists have questioned whether altering a person's past experience is ever desirable.

items.stmt: Scientists once [th:thought] that a memory, after it had been {co:consolidated}, was essentially [g:____].
items.explain: 'Permanent form' → fixed (cố định). 'Inaccessible' (không truy cập được) sai nghĩa.

items.stmt: However, studies on {rt:rats} showed that [rc:remembering] a fearful event made the memory [g:____] for a [st:short period].
items.explain: 'Unstable' (không ổn định, dễ bị thay đổi) → vulnerable (dễ bị tổn thương/tác động).

items.stmt: This process may [ex:explain] why the [ac:accounts] given by [g:____] are often [ur:inaccurate].

ex.vi: cơ chế hợp lý (để giải thích)

items.explain: 'Eyewitness testimony' = lời khai của nhân chứng → witnesses. 'Scientists' là bẫy (có trong bài nhưng sai chỗ).

items.stmt: The research has also [en:given rise to] [g:____] that [tm:distressing memories] could be {md:deliberately modified},
items.explain: 'Raised hopes' → optimism (sự lạc quan). 'Scepticism' (hoài nghi) là trái nghĩa – nghĩ đến các nhà đạo đức học nhưng đó là ý khác.

items.stmt: although [ts:tests on patients] have [sf:up to now] given [g:____] results.
items.explain: 'Inconsistent results' → mixed (lẫn lộn, lúc được lúc không). 'Conclusive' (có tính kết luận) là trái nghĩa.

sets.title: Why languages fall silent
sets.topic: Ngôn ngữ học · ngôn ngữ tuyệt chủng
sets.passage: Of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken today, linguists estimate that as many as half may fall silent by the end of this century. The conventional explanation attributes this decline to globalisation, yet the historical record suggests a more complicated picture. Languages have always vanished; what is unprecedented is the pace. Moreover, the decisive factor is seldom outright prohibition. Far more often, parents in minority communities voluntarily abandon their ancestral tongue, reasoning that fluency in a dominant language will secure their children's prospects. This choice, rational at the level of the individual household, produces a collective loss that no single family intended. Revitalisation efforts have yielded mixed results. Hebrew, revived as an everyday language in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, is frequently cited as proof that extinction can be reversed, but its case is arguably exceptional: its revival coincided with the founding of a nation-state that had compelling ideological reasons to promote it. Communities lacking such institutional backing have generally found it far harder to persuade younger speakers that the effort is worthwhile.

items.stmt: What does the writer consider [un:new] about the [ls:disappearance] of languages today?
options: the number of languages that are affected
the speed at which it is happening
the involvement of governments
the fact that it happens at all
items.explain: 'Languages have always vanished' loại D. Cái mới (unprecedented) là 'the pace' = tốc độ → B.

items.stmt: According to the writer, the [mc:main cause] of language decline is usually
options: official bans on minority languages
decisions made freely by parents
a shortage of written materials
the movement of people to cities
items.explain: 'Seldom outright prohibition' loại A. 'Far more often, parents ... voluntarily abandon' → B.

items.stmt: What point does the writer make about the [ch:decision] taken by {pa:parents}?
options: It is usually made under pressure from the authorities.
It makes sense for each family but has an effect nobody wanted.
It rarely benefits the children involved.
It is based on inaccurate information about the future.
items.explain: Câu 'rational at the level of the individual household, produces a collective loss that no single family intended' được paraphrase gần như toàn bộ trong B.

items.stmt: The writer refers to the [rs:restoration] of {hb:Hebrew} in order to
options: show that any language can be saved with enough effort
suggest that a well-known example may not be typical
criticise the methods used by the state
explain why young people reject minority languages
items.explain: A là quan điểm của người khác ('frequently cited as proof'); tác giả phản bác bằng 'but ... arguably exceptional' → B.

items.stmt: What [di:difficulty] do communities [wi:without official support] usually face?

wi.vi: thiếu sự hậu thuẫn của thể chế

options: finding qualified teachers
competing with other minority languages
convincing the young that the effort is worthwhile
opposition from national governments
items.explain: 'Far harder to persuade younger speakers that the effort is worthwhile' → C.

sets.title: Learning from nature: biomimicry
sets.topic: Kỹ thuật · thiết kế mô phỏng sinh học
sets.passage: Engineers have long borrowed ideas from nature, but the deliberate, systematic study of biological solutions – now often called biomimicry – has gained momentum only in recent decades. Its advocates point to a growing list of successes. The structure of termite mounds, which maintain a remarkably stable internal temperature without any external energy source, informed the design of an office complex in Zimbabwe that uses a fraction of the electricity consumed by conventionally cooled buildings of similar size. The microscopic texture of sharkskin, which discourages bacteria from settling, has been reproduced on hospital surfaces. Critics, however, caution against romanticising the natural world. Evolution does not produce optimal designs; it produces structures that are merely adequate for an organism's survival, and these are constrained by the materials and developmental pathways available. A bird's wing, for instance, must also serve functions irrelevant to an aircraft. The most productive approach, these critics suggest, is not to copy nature directly but to extract the underlying principle and adapt it to human requirements.

items.stmt: Although engineers have {lb:long borrowed} ideas from nature, a [g:____] approach to this has [gm:become popular] [rc:only lately].

rc.vi: chỉ trong vài thập kỷ gần đây

items.explain: 'Deliberate, systematic' → methodical (có phương pháp). 'Commercial' không có trong bài.

items.stmt: An office building in {zb:Zimbabwe}, [ms:based on] {tm:termite mounds}, uses [fl:much less] [g:____] than [cp:comparable] buildings.
items.explain: 'Electricity' → power. 'Maintenance' (bảo trì) không được nhắc.

items.stmt: {cr:Critics} [wa:warn] that evolution creates designs that are [on:no more than] [g:____] for {sv:survival}.
items.explain: 'Merely adequate' → sufficient (vừa đủ). 'Perfect' bị phủ định bởi 'does not produce optimal designs'.

items.stmt: Such designs are also [lm:limited] by the [g:____] and developmental routes that are {av:available}.
items.explain: 'Constrained by the materials and developmental pathways available' → materials.

items.stmt: Instead of [cy:imitating] nature {di:directly}, engineers should [ex:draw out] the basic [g:____] and {ad:adapt} it.
items.explain: 'Extract the underlying principle' → principle. 'Structure' là bẫy: có trong bài nhưng ở ý khác.

sets.title: The paradox of choice revisited
sets.topic: Tâm lý học · hành vi người tiêu dùng
sets.passage: In a frequently quoted experiment conducted in a Californian supermarket, shoppers who were offered a tasting table of twenty-four varieties of jam were considerably less likely to make a purchase than those offered only six. The finding seemed to confirm an intuition that had long circulated among marketing professionals: that an abundance of options can paralyse rather than liberate. Subsequent research, however, has proved difficult to reconcile with this tidy conclusion. A meta-analysis combining the results of some fifty studies found that the average effect of increasing choice was close to zero, with some experiments reporting the opposite pattern. Researchers have since attempted to identify the circumstances under which an excess of options does become burdensome. The effect appears strongest when consumers lack clear preferences, when the alternatives are difficult to compare, and when they are under pressure to decide quickly. Such qualifications are rarely mentioned in the popular books that have turned the original study into a parable about modern life.

items.stmt: The results of the {jm:jam} experiment [sp:came as a surprise to] [me:people in marketing].
items.explain: Kết quả 'confirm an intuition' (xác nhận trực giác vốn có) của dân marketing → không hề bất ngờ → FALSE.

items.stmt: [ls:Later studies] have [cs:consistently supported] the original finding.
items.explain: 'Difficult to reconcile with this tidy conclusion' + hiệu ứng trung bình gần bằng 0 → không ủng hộ nhất quán → FALSE.

items.stmt: {st:Some experiments} found that [mo:offering more options] had the [rv:reverse] effect.
items.explain: 'Some experiments reporting the opposite pattern' → TRUE.

items.stmt: [tc:Too much choice] is [ml:most likely] to cause difficulty when shoppers are [un:unsure what they want].
items.explain: 'The effect appears strongest when consumers lack clear preferences' → TRUE.

items.stmt: The [rs:researchers who ran the original study] [ob:object to] the way their work has been [po:popularised].

ob.vi: bài không nói ý kiến của nhóm nghiên cứu gốc

items.explain: Bài phê bình các cuốn sách phổ thông, nhưng không hề nói nhóm nghiên cứu gốc phản đối → NOT GIVEN. Đừng nhầm ý của TÁC GIẢ với ý của nhân vật khác.

sets.title: The ambiguous triumph of farming
sets.topic: Khảo cổ học · nguồn gốc nông nghiệp
sets.passage: The transition from foraging to farming, which began in south-west Asia roughly twelve thousand years ago, was long portrayed as a triumph of human ingenuity: once people grasped that seeds could be planted, the advantages of a settled life were supposedly so obvious that the new practice spread rapidly. Archaeological evidence now suggests a slower and more ambiguous process. Wild cereals were cultivated for well over a millennium before they display the physical changes associated with full domestication, and many communities moved back and forth between farming and foraging for generations. Nor were the benefits self-evident. Skeletal remains from early agricultural villages frequently show signs of nutritional deficiency and reduced stature compared with those of contemporary hunter-gatherers, while dense settlements encouraged the spread of infectious disease. Why, then, did farming prevail? One influential answer is that it supported higher population densities: even if individual farmers were less healthy, farming communities could simply outnumber their neighbours. Agriculture, on this view, succeeded not because it improved lives but because it multiplied them.

items.stmt: The [sh:shift] from foraging to farming was [lp:for a long time presented] as proof of human [g:____].
items.explain: 'Ingenuity' → inventiveness (óc sáng tạo).

items.stmt: It was [as:assumed] that the new practice had {sp:spread} in a [g:____] manner.
items.explain: 'Spread rapidly' → swift. 'Gradual' là bẫy: đó là quan điểm MỚI ('slower'), không phải quan điểm cũ được hỏi.

items.stmt: However, [sk:bones found] in early farming villages suggest that people there were often [g:____] and [sm:shorter] than hunter-gatherers.
items.explain: 'Nutritional deficiency' → malnourished (suy dinh dưỡng). 'Healthier' trái nghĩa.

items.stmt: In addition, [cr:crowded villages] helped [g:____] to {sp:spread}.
items.explain: 'Infectious disease' → illnesses.

items.stmt: Farming may have {pv:prevail}ed because it [ss:made possible] larger [g:____], even if {lh:individual farmers} were [hl:in poorer health].

g.vi: mật độ dân số cao hơn

items.explain: 'Higher population densities' / 'multiplied them' → populations. 'Harvests' (mùa màng) không được nhắc.

sets.title: A short history of peer review
sets.topic: Lịch sử khoa học · xuất bản học thuật
sets.passage: It is commonly assumed that peer review – the practice of submitting research to the scrutiny of independent experts before publication – has been a cornerstone of science since its origins. In fact, the system in its modern form is surprisingly recent. When the Royal Society began publishing its Philosophical Transactions in 1665, decisions about what to print rested largely with the editor, and for much of the following two centuries most journals operated on a similar basis. Systematic external refereeing became widespread only after the Second World War, when a dramatic expansion in the number of submissions made it impossible for editors to evaluate every manuscript themselves. Even the journal Nature did not adopt formal peer review for all its papers until the 1970s. Historians who draw attention to this chronology are not, for the most part, seeking to discredit the practice. Their point is rather that the authority now attached to it owes as much to institutional necessity as to any demonstrated ability to separate sound research from flawed.

items.stmt: What [mi:widespread belief] does the writer challenge at the start of the passage?
options: that peer review slows down scientific progress
that peer review is as old as science itself
that early journals published very little research
that experts rarely agree with one another
items.explain: 'Has been a cornerstone of science since its origins' rồi bị phản bác bằng 'In fact ... surprisingly recent' → B.

items.stmt: In the [ey:first years] of {pt:Philosophical Transactions}, decisions about publication were made [ma:mainly] by
options: a committee of Society members
independent specialists
the editor
the authors themselves
items.explain: 'Rested largely with the editor' → C. B (independent experts) là đặc điểm của peer review hiện đại – bẫy.

items.stmt: According to the writer, {er:external refereeing} [sp:became common] [af:after 1945] because
options: editors could no longer assess the growing number of papers
scientists demanded fairer treatment
fraud had damaged the reputation of journals
governments made it a condition of funding
para: dramatic expansion in the number of submissions
items.explain: Lý do nằm ngay sau 'when ...' → A. Các lựa chọn khác không được nhắc.

items.stmt: The writer mentions {na:Nature} to show that {fp:formal peer review} was [ad:introduced]
options: surprisingly late, even by a leading journal
first of all by that journal
against the wishes of most scientists
less strictly there than at other journals
para: Even ... did not adopt ... until the 1970s
items.explain: Từ 'Even' cho thấy ngay cả tạp chí hàng đầu cũng áp dụng muộn → A.

items.stmt: What is the [ma:main aim] of the {hi:historians} mentioned at the end?
options: to show that peer review has no real value
to suggest that its prestige partly reflects practical necessity
to propose an alternative to peer review
to defend the traditional role of editors
items.explain: A bị phủ định bởi 'not ... seeking to discredit'. Ý chính: uy tín (authority) đến một phần từ nhu cầu thể chế → B.

sets.title: The ironies of automation
sets.topic: Công nghệ · tự động hóa và con người
sets.passage: Automation is usually justified on the grounds that machines are less prone to error than people. Yet the introduction of automated systems frequently creates a new category of mistake. Studies of pilots, radiologists and process-plant operators have documented a tendency, known as automation bias, for human supervisors to accept a system's recommendations without adequate scrutiny, even when contradictory information is readily available. Paradoxically, the more reliable a system is, the more pronounced this tendency becomes: operators who rarely see the machine fail gradually lose the habit of checking it. A related difficulty is the erosion of manual skills. When automation does break down, it typically does so in unusual circumstances that its designers failed to anticipate – precisely the situations in which an experienced human would be most valuable, and in which a deskilled one is least capable of intervening. Some researchers therefore advocate designs that keep operators actively engaged, for example by requiring them to perform certain tasks manually at regular intervals, even at some cost to efficiency.

items.stmt: Automation is [jf:generally defended] on the basis that it reduces [g:____].
items.explain: 'Less prone to error' → giảm inaccuracies (sai sót).

items.stmt: {su:Human supervisors} may {ac:accept} a system's [rc:advice] without proper [g:____].
items.explain: 'Scrutiny' → examination. 'Training' là bẫy: hợp ngữ pháp nhưng không có trong bài.

items.stmt: [pd:Strangely], this tendency becomes [wo:stronger] as systems become more [g:____].
items.explain: 'Reliable' → dependable. 'Complex' nghe hợp lý nhưng bài không nói.

items.stmt: When automation [fa:fails], it usually does so in [g:____] situations, where [ex:an experienced person] would be [mo:most useful].
items.explain: 'Unusual circumstances that its designers failed to anticipate' → unforeseen. 'Routine' trái nghĩa.

items.stmt: Some researchers [rc:recommend] requiring operators to carry out certain tasks [mn:by hand] [g:____].
items.explain: 'At regular intervals' → periodically. 'Permanently' sai vì chỉ là thỉnh thoảng định kỳ.

sets.title: Why new roads fill up
sets.topic: Quy hoạch đô thị · giao thông
sets.passage: For much of the twentieth century, traffic engineers approached congestion as a straightforward problem of supply: if roads were overcrowded, the remedy was to build more of them. Yet a growing body of evidence indicates that additional capacity tends to generate additional traffic. When a new lane is opened, journeys that drivers previously avoided – because they were inconvenient, or could be made by public transport – suddenly become attractive, and within a few years the road is frequently as congested as before. This phenomenon, known as induced demand, was described in outline as early as the 1930s, but it was not until the 1990s that transport departments began to take it seriously in their forecasts. The converse also seems to hold. Studies of cities where major roads have been closed, whether through deliberate policy or as a result of disasters, report that a proportion of the displaced traffic simply disappears rather than overwhelming neighbouring streets. Such findings remain counterintuitive to many motorists, and politicians have generally been reluctant to act on them.

items.stmt: Twentieth-century {te:traffic engineers} [rg:treated] congestion as a [cx:complicated] problem.
items.explain: 'Straightforward' (đơn giản) trái nghĩa với 'complicated' → FALSE.

items.stmt: Adding [rc:road capacity] [of:often] leads to congestion [sb:returning to its earlier level].
items.explain: 'Frequently as congested as before' → TRUE.

items.stmt: {id:Induced demand} was [fi:first identified] in the {ys:1990s}.
items.explain: Đã được mô tả từ 1930s; 1990s chỉ là lúc được 'take seriously'. Bẫy: năm 1990s có trong bài nhưng gắn với ý khác → FALSE.

items.stmt: When major roads are {cl:closed}, [al:all of the traffic] moves onto [ns:nearby streets].
items.explain: 'A proportion of the displaced traffic simply disappears rather than overwhelming neighbouring streets' → không phải tất cả → FALSE.

items.stmt: Closures caused by {ds:disasters} have had [ml:longer-lasting effects] than [pl:planned closures].

ml.vi: bài không so sánh độ bền của tác động

items.explain: Bài nhắc cả hai loại đóng đường nhưng KHÔNG so sánh chúng → NOT GIVEN. Câu so sánh hơn mà bài không so sánh = dấu hiệu NG.

sets.title: In defence of boredom
sets.topic: Tâm lý học · quan điểm tác giả
sets.passage: Boredom has rarely enjoyed a good reputation. Moralists have long treated it as a symptom of idleness, and modern employers regard it chiefly as a threat to productivity. In my view, both attitudes misunderstand its function. Boredom is best understood not as an absence of stimulation but as a signal that our current activity has ceased to engage us meaningfully – in that sense it resembles pain, which is unpleasant precisely because it prompts us to act. Some psychologists have gone further, claiming that periods of tedium are a precondition for creativity. The evidence for this is suggestive rather than conclusive: laboratory studies in which participants who first completed a dull task subsequently generated more inventive ideas have proved difficult to replicate. What seems beyond dispute, however, is that the habit of reaching for a phone at the first hint of tedium deprives people of the opportunity to discover what they actually wish to do. Schools that schedule every minute of a child's day may therefore be doing more harm than good, though I would not go so far as to recommend that lessons be made deliberately monotonous.

items.stmt: The writer [ag:shares] the [tr:traditional view] that boredom is a sign of [la:laziness].

ag.vi: hiểu sai (tác giả không đồng tình)

tr.vi: các nhà đạo đức từ lâu đã coi

items.explain: Tác giả nói 'both attitudes misunderstand its function' → không đồng ý với quan điểm truyền thống → NO.

items.stmt: The writer [cm:likens] {bo:boredom} to [ph:an unpleasant bodily feeling] that [mo:pushes us into action].
items.explain: 'It resembles pain, which is unpleasant precisely because it prompts us to act' → YES.

items.stmt: It has been [fp:firmly established] that boredom is [nc:necessary for] {cr:creativity}.

fp.vi: mang tính gợi ý chứ chưa kết luận

items.explain: Bằng chứng 'suggestive rather than conclusive', thí nghiệm 'difficult to replicate' → chưa được chứng minh chắc chắn → NO.

items.stmt: [mo:Most] {or:schools} now [fi:fill] every minute of children's time.

mo.vi: bài không nói 'phần lớn' trường học

items.explain: Tác giả chỉ nói về 'Schools that schedule every minute' (những trường làm vậy), không nói bao nhiêu trường làm vậy → NOT GIVEN.

items.stmt: The writer [re:advises] that lessons should be made [db:intentionally dull].
items.explain: 'I would not go so far as to recommend...' = tác giả KHÔNG khuyên như vậy → NO. Bẫy: từ 'recommend' có trong bài nhưng bị phủ định.

sets.title: The problem of the last mile
sets.passage: In freight logistics, the final stage of a journey – the movement of goods from a local depot to the customer's door – is notoriously the most expensive. Industry estimates commonly attribute more than half of total delivery costs to this 'last mile', largely because vehicles must make numerous small drops along unpredictable routes, often failing to find anyone at home. The rapid expansion of online retail has intensified the problem, while also generating congestion and emissions in residential streets that were never designed for heavy commercial traffic. Firms have experimented with a variety of remedies. Parcel lockers, located at stations and supermarkets, allow customers to collect items at their convenience and enable couriers to consolidate dozens of deliveries into a single stop. Some cities have established micro-hubs from which cargo bicycles complete the final leg, an approach that appears particularly effective in dense historic centres. Autonomous delivery robots have attracted considerable publicity, but their deployment remains confined to small trials, partly because regulators are uncertain how they should share pavements with pedestrians.

items.stmt: The {fs:final stage} of delivery is [kn:well known] to be the [g:____] part of the journey.
items.explain: 'Most expensive' → costliest. 'Slowest' không được nhắc.

items.stmt: This is [ma:mainly] because drivers make [nu:many small stops] and [of:frequently] discover that [g:____] are not at home.

g.vi: (không có) ai ở nhà = người nhận

items.explain: Người không có nhà là người nhận hàng → recipients. 'Couriers' (người giao) là bẫy.

items.stmt: The [gr:growth] of [on:internet shopping] has made the problem worse and [br:brought] more [g:____] to residential streets.
items.explain: 'Emissions' (khí thải) → pollution. 'Noise' không có trong bài.

sets.title: Science by the crowd
sets.passage: Over the past two decades, so-called citizen science – research in which members of the public collect or analyse data – has grown from a curiosity into a significant contributor to several disciplines. Amateur birdwatchers now supply much of the information used to track changes in bird populations, and online volunteers have classified millions of galaxy images that professional astronomers could never have examined unaided. Sceptics initially questioned the reliability of such data, arguing that untrained observers would inevitably make errors. Studies comparing volunteer and expert classifications have largely allayed these fears, provided that tasks are clearly defined and each item is examined by several participants, so that individual mistakes cancel one another out. A subtler concern is that projects tend to recruit from a narrow demographic: participants are disproportionately well educated and affluent, which may skew both the questions that are asked and the locations from which data are gathered. Proponents argue that the greatest benefit of citizen science may lie not in the data at all but in the scientific literacy it fosters, though this claim has so far received little systematic investigation.

items.explain: 'Grown from a curiosity into a significant contributor to several disciplines' → A. C sai vì bài không nói thay thế chuyên gia.

sets.title: What happens to memories at night
sets.topic: Khoa học thần kinh · giấc ngủ
sets.passage: Scientists have long suspected that sleep plays a role in memory, but only recently have they begun to understand the mechanism. During deep, slow-wave sleep, the hippocampus – a structure that temporarily stores new experiences – appears to replay the day's events, transferring them to the cortex, where they are integrated with existing knowledge. Experiments in which volunteers learned word pairs before either sleeping or remaining awake have repeatedly found that those who slept recalled more the following morning. Intriguingly, sleep does not merely preserve memories; it seems to reorganise them. In one well-known study, participants who slept were more than twice as likely as those who stayed awake to discover a hidden rule that simplified a numerical task. Such findings have practical implications. Students who sacrifice sleep to revise late into the night may undermine the very learning they are trying to secure, and shift workers, whose sleep is frequently disrupted, may be at a particular disadvantage when acquiring new skills.

items.stmt: Scientists have {su:long suspected} a link between sleep and memory, but the [g:____] [in:behind it] has [on:only lately] become clearer.
items.explain: 'Mechanism' (cơ chế) → process. 'Location' sai nghĩa.

items.stmt: During [ds:the deepest kind of sleep], the hippocampus, which holds new experiences [te:for a short time], {rp:replay}s them so they can be [g:____] with existing knowledge.
items.explain: 'Integrated with existing knowledge' → combined. 'Compared' là bẫy về nghĩa.

items.stmt: Volunteers who slept after learning {wp:word pairs} showed better [g:____] [nm:the next day].
items.explain: 'Recalled more' → khả năng ghi nhớ tốt hơn = retention. 'Attention' (sự chú ý) không phải ý của bài.

items.explain: 'Hidden rule' → một quy luật/khuôn mẫu = pattern.

items.stmt: {st:Students} who [sa:give up] sleep in order to [rv:study] may [g:____] their own learning.
items.explain: 'Undermine' → damage. 'Improve' trái nghĩa.

sets.title: The box that changed trade
sets.passage: Before the 1950s, loading a cargo ship was a slow and labour-intensive business. Goods arrived at the docks in sacks, barrels and crates of every size, and gangs of dockworkers stowed them by hand, a process that could keep a vessel in port for a week or more. The American trucking entrepreneur Malcom McLean is generally credited with demonstrating that standardised steel boxes, which could be lifted directly from lorry to ship, would transform this process. His first converted tanker sailed from Newark to Houston in 1956. The economic consequences were not immediate. Ports had to be rebuilt with specialised cranes and vast storage areas, and dockworkers' unions, fearing mass redundancies, resisted the change for years. Only after international standards for container dimensions were agreed in the late 1960s did the system begin to spread worldwide. Economists still disagree about how much of the subsequent growth in world trade can be attributed to containerisation, but one widely cited study concluded that its effect was larger than that of all trade agreements of the period combined.

items.stmt: Before containers, loading could [kp:keep a ship] in port for [mt:seven days or longer].
items.explain: 'A week or more' = seven days or longer → TRUE.

items.explain: 'Generally credited with demonstrating' ≠ 'first to suggest'. Bài không nói ai là người đề xuất đầu tiên → NOT GIVEN.

items.explain: 'The economic consequences were not immediate' → FALSE.

sets.title: A second life for batteries
sets.topic: Công nghệ · tái chế pin lithium
sets.passage: As electric vehicles multiply, attention is turning to what will happen to their batteries once they reach the end of their useful lives. Lithium-ion batteries contain valuable metals such as cobalt, nickel and lithium, yet at present only a modest proportion are recycled, in part because their designs vary so widely between manufacturers that disassembly cannot easily be automated. The two dominant recovery methods each involve compromises. Pyrometallurgy, which smelts batteries at high temperatures, is robust and tolerant of mixed inputs, but it consumes large amounts of energy and loses much of the lithium. Hydrometallurgy, which dissolves the materials in chemical solutions, recovers a wider range of metals but generates liquid waste that must be carefully treated. A third option, known as direct recycling, attempts to restore the cathode material without breaking it down into its constituent elements; it promises substantial savings but remains largely confined to the laboratory. Many analysts argue that the most effective intervention would be regulatory: requiring manufacturers to standardise designs and label battery chemistry clearly would make every recycling method cheaper.

items.stmt: Only a [sm:small share] of batteries are recycled, [pa:partly] because [va:large differences] in design make it hard to [g:____] taking them apart.
items.explain: 'Cannot easily be automated' → khó mechanise (cơ giới hóa). 'Prohibit' sai nghĩa.

items.stmt: {py:Pyrometallurgy} can [ha:cope with] mixed materials but [us:uses up] a great deal of [g:____].
items.explain: 'Consumes large amounts of energy' → power. 'Water' là bẫy (liên tưởng tới dung dịch ở phương pháp sau).

items.stmt: {hy:Hydrometallurgy} recovers [mo:more kinds of metal] but [ge:produces] [g:____] that needs careful treatment.
items.explain: 'Liquid waste' → effluent (nước thải) – từ uncommon rất hay gặp trong IELTS.

items.stmt: {dr:Direct recycling} could [cu:reduce costs] [sb:considerably], but it is still mostly [g:____].

items.explain: 'Label battery chemistry clearly' → identification (việc ghi rõ/nhận diện).

sets.title: When to trust your gut
sets.topic: Tâm lý học · trực giác chuyên gia
sets.passage: It is often said that experts rely on intuition rather than deliberate reasoning, and in many fields this description is accurate. An experienced firefighter may sense that a building is about to collapse without being able to explain why; a chess master may glance at a board and immediately see the strongest move. Yet I believe the popular enthusiasm for 'trusting your gut' has outrun the evidence. Intuition is reliable only in environments that are sufficiently regular and that provide rapid, unambiguous feedback, conditions that allow the patterns underlying expert judgement to be learned. Chess satisfies both requirements; long-term political forecasting satisfies neither, and it is no coincidence that the confident predictions of political pundits have been shown to be scarcely more accurate than chance. The difficulty is that subjective confidence is a poor guide to accuracy: an intuition feels equally compelling whether or not it rests on genuine expertise. Organisations would therefore be wise to ask not how certain their experts feel, but whether the domain in which they work is one in which skill can be acquired at all.

items.stmt: The writer [ac:accepts] that in [so:a number of areas], experts {in:rely on intuition}.
items.explain: 'In many fields this description is accurate' → tác giả thừa nhận → YES.

pe.vi: sự nhiệt tình của công chúng
